title: Aurelius - Private VPC Deep Dive: Networking & Runtime
summary: Deep technical session covering Private VPC networking design and how Redwood runtime behaves inside PrivateLink/NAT architectures. Discussed DNS, subnets, route tables, PrivateLink vs NAT gateway tradeoffs, egress requirements for model variants, and performance considerations (latency/throughput) for KV cache, batching, and quantized models. Action items: share network diagrams, run a small perf benchmark inside customer's VPC, and provide onboarding checklist and security docs.
topics: Egress requirements for model downloads and telemetry
KV cache and prefix caching latency impact
Audit logs, KMS, and compliance considerations
transcript:
[00:00] Jordan: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, we have about an hour, wanted to run through the private VPC design and then dive into runtime perf questions. I'm Jordan from Redwood.
[00:06] Mark: Thanks, Jordan. We have our infra folks and security on — Sofia and Priya are here.
[00:12] Priya Nair (SE): Hi all, I'm Priya, I'll take the deep tech parts on networking and runtime. Quick agenda: architecture, networking paths, and then perf numbers and blind spots.
[00:22] Sofia: Sounds good. We're particularly interested in PrivateLink and what egress we need — we prefer no internet egress if possible.
[00:28] Jordan: Totally, we've done fully private installs. We'll explain two patterns: PrivateLink (interface endpoints) where control plane talks over AWS PrivateLink to your VPC — that keeps traffic inside the AWS backbone — and a VPC-proxy pattern where you allow limited egress for model downloads, telemetry to an S3 presigned URL or to our mirror.
[00:45] Tom: When you say "no egress" — does that mean model weights never leave the customer's network? How do model updates work?
[00:51] Priya Nair: Good question. For Private deployments we support two modes: 1) Model weights are pulled from Redwood-hosted S3 via a signed, short-lived url — that requires egress to S3 endpoints (or a VPC endpoint to S3). 2) You can mirror the model artifacts into your own S3 and we pull from there with IAM roles — that can be fully private. The control plane can be PrivateLink-only.
[01:12] Priya G (customer): For audits we want to prove nothing crossed the public internet. Option 2 is preferred.
[01:17] Evan Park (Redwood): Also note, if you use PrivateLink the control/control-plane API calls hit our endpoint in your VPC over interface ENIs, and for runtime traffic we can run a private runtime inside your VPC so tokens never leave.
[01:30] Mark: Okay, let's talk networking specifics — subnets, route tables, NAT.
[01:34] Priya Nair: Typical pattern: put the runtime instances in private subnets (no IGW), attach route to NAT only if you need external egress. Alternatively, use VPC endpoints (Gateway type for S3, Interface type for PrivateLink, ECR). For PrivateLink control plane you create an interface endpoint in the customer VPC and we accept connections on the service side.
[01:53] Sofia: What's the behavior for DNS? We use conditional forwarding for internal domains and have internal resolver clusters.
[01:59] Priya Nair: With interface endpoints, AWS creates private DNS names — route 53 resolver rules still apply. One gotcha: if you have an on-prem forwarding chain, ensure the resolver can handle the private endpoint hostnames; otherwise the ENI won't resolve. We recommend testing with "dig" against the VPC resolver and checking the interface endpoint IPs.
[02:20] Jordan: Also callout: some customers use Transit Gateway and multiple accounts; with TGW you can centralize endpoints but watch the propagation of route tables for ENI reachability.
[02:30] Tom: How do we handle high throughput? Our inference volume is bursty — thousands of rps for short windows.
[02:36] Priya Nair: On throughput, runtime scales horizontally. Primary constraints are VPC ENI limits and per-AZ ENI bandwidth. For PrivateLink, each interface endpoint has bandwidth characteristics; the more ENIs, the more parallel throughput. We recommend spreading runtime across multiple subnets/AZs and sizing ENIs appropriately.
[02:57] Mark: Any latency hit from PrivateLink compared to public internet?
[03:01] Priya Nair: Usually PrivateLink is slightly faster and more predictable because it's inside the AWS network; main added hop is the interface ENI and the service side NLB we use. Observed median added latency is generally sub-ms to a few ms depending on AZ hops, but we should test from your region/account.
[03:17] Sofia: We care about p50 and p99 for small and long sequences — especially for chat-like workloads where we rely on KV cache.
[03:25] Priya Nair: Right. KV cache is in-memory per runtime instance. The key latency component is the time to fetch from the cache vs the compute time. If cache hits are high, end-to-end latency drops because the model doesn't need to recompute tokens. Network latency between your app and the runtime is separate — keep that under 5–10ms if you're aiming for low RT.
[03:44] Jordan: Could you walk through end-to-end request path — client -> runtime -> model?
[03:48] Priya Nair: Sure: client -> your app -> VPC routing -> runtime instance (ENI) -> local KV cache lookup -> model forward. If KV miss and we use a multi-stage model pipeline (e.g., reranker on a different instance), that can add cross-instance network calls — we try to colocate cache and model to avoid that.
[04:06] Tom: For batching — how do you guarantee latency SLOs? We have a 200ms p50 requirement for short queries.
[04:12] Priya Nair: We offer adaptive batching with a latency cap. The runtime continuously estimates queue times and dynamically forms batches up to a size that meets the latency target. There's a tradeoff: bigger batches improve throughput and cost but increase tail latency. We can set per-route SLOs and have overflow to a lower-cost model or fast fallback.
[04:30] Mark: Can we control batch sizes per model or per route?
[04:33] Priya Nair: Yes — config at the route level: max_batch_size, max_batch_latency_ms, and preferred quantization profile. We recommend starting with conservative defaults and tuning with a short benchmark.
[04:44] Sofia: Regarding quantization — we want low latency but not at the cost of hallucinations. What's your guidance?
[04:49] Evan Park: Quantization reduces memory and compute — for many transformer models 4-bit or 8-bit gives major perf wins with minimal quality loss, but it depends on the model. For sensitive gen tasks we run evals on your prompt sets to see quality drift. We provide quantization profiles and can roll out A/B tests — keep the unquantized model as a fallback for critical traffic.
[05:08] Tom: Any specific networking impacts of quantized models?
[05:11] Priya Nair: Only indirect: smaller models mean less memory pressure and better cache locality. No special network changes. But if quantized models allow more concurrency per host, you'll see different ENI throughput usage patterns.
[05:22] Mark: On the VPC endpoints, do we need to open outbound rules or security groups?
[05:26] Priya Nair: Interface endpoints require security groups; allow inbound from your runtime subnets. For gateway endpoints (S3), it's route table-based and doesn't use SGs. For PrivateLink, you'll create an interface endpoint in the consuming account and attach an SG that permits traffic. We also recommend SCPs and IAM role restrictions if you're locking down access.
[05:46] Priya G (customer): Our compliance team asked about audit logs and KMS — can logs be shipped to our Splunk and keys be customer-managed?
[05:53] Jordan: Yes — audit logs can be emitted to CloudWatch or your S3; from there you can forward to Splunk. KMS: we support customer-managed keys (CMKs) for model artifact encryption and in-flight TLS; for HSM-level controls we have options in the Private bundle.
[06:08] Sofia: How is telemetry handled? Is there any PII that leaves the VPC?
[06:13] Evan Park: Telemetry (metrics/traces) can be configured to point to your observability endpoints; by default lightweight metrics go to the control plane, but for Private installs you can opt to keep telemetry internal or send scrubbed metrics only. We'll provide a telemetry config that enumerates what leaves.
[06:29] Mark: Let's get a bit more concrete — can you share the typical security group rules and a sample route table?
[06:35] Priya Nair: Sure; here's a short example: Runtime SG: allow inbound TCP 443 from your app subnet CIDRs and from interface endpoint SG; allow outbound to S3 VPC endpoint and to ECR endpoint; no IGW route. Route table: private subnet routes point to NAT only if egress needed; otherwise no 0.0.0.0/0. For connectivity to control plane via PrivateLink, the interface endpoint sits in the private subnet and resolves to private DNS name. We'll share a sample diagram after the call.
[07:00] Mark: Can we do a short perf test inside our account? We want to measure p50/p95 for a 64-token chat payload and a 512-token completion.
[07:08] Jordan: Yes, that's exactly the benchmark we suggest. Action: we'll provide a benchmarking harness and a small CloudFormation/Terraform module to spin up the runtime with the correct SGs and endpoints.
[07:18] Tom: For the KV cache, if we have sharded cache across instances, is there a consistency model we need to worry about?
[07:25] Priya Nair: Cache is per-host; we don't provide a global coherent cache across hosts by default. We rely on deterministic routing (sticky sessions) so a given conversational session lands on the same instance and benefits from local cache. For cross-host sharing we can look at a managed cache like Redis in your VPC but that introduces network round trips and latency.
[07:44] Sofia: About ENI limits — what happens when we hit AWS ENI quotas? Is there graceful degradation?
[07:50] Evan Park: If you hit ENI limits in an AZ, the autoscaler will place instances in other AZs; we also can fall back to hosted capacity if you have hybrid setup (redwood Dedicated burst). We monitor and alert on ENI exhaustion and can provide quota planning guidance.
[08:08] Mark: Any specific NAT costs we should watch out for with model downloads?
[08:12] Priya Nair: NAT gateways incur per-GB egress costs; using gateway endpoints to S3 or mirroring artifacts into your private S3 avoids NAT charges. Also ECR pulls can use VPC endpoints.
[08:25] Jordan: Let's capture next steps and owners.
[08:29] Priya Nair: I'll share the network diagram, sample SGs, and terraform module. Jordan will share pricing and the onboarding checklist. Tom and Mark will run the perf harness and share results.
[08:41] Mark: Good — also please include the security pack: SOC 2 docs, encryption details, and the KMS setup guide.
[08:48] Jordan: We'll send that.
[08:51] Sofia: Quick one — is there any reason to prefer NAT instance vs NAT gateway?
[08:55] Priya Nair: Only if you need fine-grained packet inspection or custom routing logic; NAT instances are manageable but less scalable and more ops burden. We usually recommend NAT gateway or VPC endpoints to reduce egress.
[09:06] Tom: If we want to test latency differences between quantized vs full-precision, how long does it take to stage a model?
[09:12] Evan Park: Staging a model is minutes for smaller models, hours for very large >1TB weight sets if you need to transfer. But for the A/B experiments we typically stage in parallel and route 5–10% traffic to the quantized variant.
[09:26] Jordan: Thanks everyone — we'll recap and follow up with artifacts.
[09:30] Priya Nair: End of recording.

Note: transcription has minor errors (speaker overlaps, occasional word swaps). Links referenced during call: - Private VPC onboarding doc: https://redwood.ai/docs/private-vpc - Terraform module (sample): https://github.com/redwood-inference/terraform-private-vpc-sample
